storm.summary_layperson: A cluster of weak storms is sliding away to the north-northeast, so no fresh storm threat is expected at the cove this evening — but because these cells are moving over land rather than crossing the Sound, the water's usual cooling effect isn't really part of the story tonight.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The Sound's cooling gap is real right now (5.8°F, air warmer than water) but shrinks to under 3°F by 7 PM as the air cools — moot here anyway, since these cells are tracking NNE over land and never cross open water on their way out.
storm.detail_html:
Radar (KOKX) shows a line of showers/weak storms 22–39 miles north to north-northeast of the cove, topping out around 41 dBZ. Instability is negligible — CAPE is only 60 J/kg — so this is pulse shower activity riding a batch of 0-6km shear (27 kt from the WNW), not an organized severe threat. Every tracked cell has a negative closing speed: they are moving away from the cove at 6–12 kt, not toward it, which is why there is no active arrival estimate this cycle.

Normally the cold Long Island Sound water (73°F) creates a shallow marine layer that can choke off storms crossing it before they reach the cove. That mechanism is bypassed today: the storm motion is NNE, parallel to and mostly inland of the Sound, so these cells were never going to traverse the cool water regardless of how strong the marine layer is. The air–water gap is 5.8°F right now and would fall under the ~5°F threshold by roughly 5:10 PM as the afternoon air cools toward evening — a real trend, just not a relevant one for cells taking this track.

Net call for the 5–10 PM window: low practical risk, better described as "moderate on paper, receding in practice." The classification reflects that reflectivity ≥35 dBZ exists within 50 miles at the scan time, but the vector on every cell points away from Riverside/Greenwich.

What would change the call: any new cell initiating closer in (within 25 mi) with a track that turns toward the cove, or renewed destabilization behind this line as the atmosphere reheats overnight — neither is currently indicated by the HRRR or the AFD, which only mentions a slight chance of additional storms well north and west of the NYC terminals.

wind.tactics_blurb: This is a wait-it-out evening, not a bank-one-side evening — light gradient wind with no real sea breeze to lean on. Stay centered, keep boat speed and mode flexible for the frequent lulls and shifts, and don't commit hard to either side.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a light gradient wind day, not a sea-breeze day. The air–water temperature difference (the "deltaT" that drives a thermal sea breeze) is 5.8°F, below the roughly 8°F gate the cove needs to build a mature sea breeze, so the sea-breeze direction-maturation correction does not apply today — the raw model wind is used as-is. Instability is negligible (CAPE 60 J/kg) and the regional pressure field is nearly flat (~1020 hPa across every station from Bridgeport to Islip), so there's no strong synoptic push either.

With no dominant thermal or pressure gradient to lean on, there's no reliable geographic favorite tonight — stay center and treat any pressure you find as short-lived rather than a side to bank on. Puffs will be scattered and won't repeat in the same spot.

Character through the window: HRRR shows wind easing from a light 6 kt southerly at 5 PM down to 3 kt by 6–7 PM as both the marine layer and any residual thermal fade, then backing sharply to ESE at 7 PM — likely outflow noise from the showers tracking north of the area rather than a real direction signal. Model coverage runs out after 7 PM this cycle, so the 8–10 PM rows are an estimate based on the observed decay trend, not direct model output; treat those hours with extra caution.

HRRR and live observations agree closely on direction right now (forecast S 187° vs. observed S 183°, a trivial 4° difference), so there's no meaningful model/obs divergence to flag.

What racers will feel: 3–6 kt is light-air sailing for the whole fleet — prioritize boat-handling smoothness and mode over trying to sail a fixed angle, expect frequent lulls, and don't be surprised if groups split simply because pressure is patchy rather than because one side is structurally favored.

data_caveats: HRRR forecast only reached 7:00 PM this cycle (8 forecast hours had fetch/parse gaps beyond that) — wind for 8:00–10:00 PM in the table is estimated from the observed decay trend, not direct model output.
